guides.name: RJ45 / 8P8C Ethernet: T568A and T568B
guides.summary: Match numbered contacts and twisted pairs when terminating Ethernet cable.
guides.useWhen: Making a straight-through patch lead or terminating a compatible data jack.
guides.why: Keeping each twisted pair together matters even when a basic continuity test passes.
guides.scope: Contact assignments for T568A/B. This is not a rear punch-down layout or a PoE injection circuit.

diagram.title: Same scheme at both ends
diagram.subtitle: Contact-number reference. Follow the exact jack's A/B label for terminal placement.

steps: Identify contact 1 using the connector drawing; plug and socket views can appear mirrored.
Use A at both ends or B at both ends for a straight-through lead. Preserve pairs 1-2, 3-6, 4-5 and 7-8.
Use a suitable cable tester; check pair assignment as well as opens and shorts.
checks: Rear IDC terminal order varies by jack; do not copy the plug's left-to-right order onto it.
An 8P8C socket may carry non-Ethernet signals. Confirm the equipment documentation before connecting it.

guides.name: UART: TX, RX and a shared reference
guides.summary: Connect a logic-level serial adapter to a compatible board console.
guides.useWhen: Reading development-board logs or sending simple commands over a short local connection.
guides.why: UART needs no separate clock wire, but both ends must agree on baud rate and framing.
guides.scope: Non-isolated, compatible logic-level UART. TX/RX labels are from each device's own perspective; no universal header order is implied.

diagram.title: Transmit meets receive
diagram.subtitle: Both devices powered appropriately; adapter VCC intentionally not connected.

steps: Confirm the target's I/O voltage and the adapter's actual TX level; a supply-voltage jumper may not change TX voltage.
Wire with power off, then select the documented baud, data bits, parity and stop bits.
Start by reading logs; garbled text often indicates framing, voltage or grounding trouble.
checks: Do not connect two TX outputs together.
RS-232 voltage levels require a transceiver; a USB connector alone does not identify an adapter's electrical interface.

guides.why: The transceiver translates the electrical levels and polarity while the UART handles byte framing.
guides.scope: Signal path only. Choose a transceiver and supply circuit from its datasheet; DTE/DCE roles determine the cable wiring.

diagram.title: Logic UART is not RS-232
diagram.subtitle: A three-wire data link still requires compatible electrical conversion.

steps: Identify both port roles and whether hardware flow control is required.
Use the equipment pinouts to select a straight-through or null-modem cable.
Match baud and framing after checking the electrical connection.

A DE9 shell does not prove a port is RS-232; similar connectors carry CAN and other interfaces.

guides.scope: Two-wire half-duplex topology with a transceiver at every node. RS-485 itself does not define Modbus addresses or a universal connector.

diagram.title: Terminate the cable ends
diagram.subtitle: Identical transceivers shown. Check polarity truth tables when mixing manufacturers.

rows: Only one transmitter active at a time
Match cable impedance at both ends
Do not add one per node
Calculate for the complete loaded bus
steps: Use a trunk with short stubs and the cable/transceiver guidance for the chosen rate.
Plan the signal reference, common-mode limits and isolation before connecting separate power systems.
Check transmit-enable timing and the protocol settings.
checks: GPIO cannot directly drive the differential pair.
Termination and bias are different circuits; modules may already contain either.

guides.name: CAN bus: controller, transceiver and termination
guides.summary: Separate the MCU's CAN signals from the two-wire physical bus.
guides.useWhen: Building a documented CAN network between development boards, robots or instruments.
guides.why: CAN controllers handle messages and arbitration; transceivers connect those controllers to CANH/CANL.
guides.scope: Conventional high-speed two-wire CAN. This is not a low-speed fault-tolerant, single-wire, OBD connector or automotive harness pinout.

diagram.title: Two cable ends, two terminators
diagram.subtitle: 120-ohm termination across CANH/CANL at each end of a 120-ohm bus.

rows: Do not swap or attach directly to GPIO
Follow the transceiver and system design
steps: Keep the trunk linear and stubs short; choose cable length and rate together.
Match bit timing; CAN FD needs compatible controllers and transceivers.
Use another active receiving node for acknowledgement during a normal transmit test.
checks: CAN does not define one universal connector or wire-color scheme.
With all power removed, two simple 120-ohm end resistors in parallel give about 60 ohms; this check alone cannot prove correct wiring.

guides.name: I2C: two shared lines with pull-ups
guides.summary: Wire SDA and SCL for compatible sensors on a short local bus.
guides.useWhen: Connecting addressed peripherals while using few MCU pins.
guides.why: Devices share data and clock lines and release them high through pull-up resistors.
guides.scope: Ordinary open-drain I2C. Connector-branded systems still require their own pinout and voltage check.

diagram.title: Pull up to a compatible logic rail
diagram.subtitle: Each line needs an effective pull-up. Existing module resistors combine in parallel.

rows: Clock; a target may stretch it
Not automatically the module power input
steps: Check addresses for collisions and configure the documented bus speed.
Determine the total pull-up resistance from all attached boards.
Choose resistance using rise-time, capacitance and sink-current limits; 4.7 kohm is not universal.
checks: A 5 V pull-up can damage a non-tolerant 3.3 V input.
Do not cross SDA and SCL. A detected address alone does not prove the correct device or power configuration.

guides.name: SPI: clock, data direction and chip select
guides.summary: Connect a host to a four-wire SPI peripheral without crossing the data roles.
guides.useWhen: Using supported displays, memory, ADCs or radio/NFC frontends.
guides.why: A shared clock times the transfer, and chip select identifies the active peripheral.
guides.scope: Conventional four-wire, active-low-CS SPI. Three-wire, daisy-chain and device-specific interfaces need their own diagrams.

diagram.title: Follow direction, not just the abbreviation
diagram.subtitle: MOSI = host out; MISO = host in. Each ordinary peripheral gets its own CS.

steps: Match I/O levels, SPI mode, bit order and maximum clock to the peripheral datasheet.
Check that shared MISO devices release the line when deselected.
Start with short wires and a conservative clock.
checks: SDI/SDO labels are local to the device. Read each signal direction.
Supply wiring and optional IRQ/reset signals are additional to the four SPI signals.

guides.name: RFID / NFC: reader, writer or emulator?
guides.summary: Choose the radio, supported tag protocol and host interface before choosing wires.
guides.useWhen: Building tag-based identification, an NDEF demonstration or your own NFC test device.
guides.why: RFID describes a broad family. A 13.56 MHz NFC module is not automatically compatible with 125 kHz or UHF tags.
guides.scope: Capability planning for documented NFC parts. Reading, writing and card emulation are separate operations; chip features do not guarantee module firmware support.

diagram.title: Two interfaces, two compatibility checks
diagram.subtitle: MCU-to-module wiring and module-to-tag radio protocol must both match.

rows: Detection is not proof of application access
A readable tag may not be writable
Supported card type and host stack
Not an automatic copy of another card
Do not transfer all features to 3917B/3919B
Host mode and supported NFC modes
Module switches and voltage circuits vary
Type-4 emulation needs the appropriate application
steps: Identify the exact module, antenna, tag technology and intended read/write/emulation role.
Choose a supported host library and verify mode support before assembling the prototype.
Use known test tags and inspect results without assuming UID detection proves full interoperability.
checks: Antenna matching and nearby metal affect operation; an arbitrary wire is not a drop-in antenna.
Module supply input, I/O voltage and RF field configuration are different specifications.
